name: Frankincense wrinkle remedy

lead: The frankincense wrinkle remedy is a traditional preparation attributed to ancient Egyptian cosmetic practice. Accounts describe frankincense gum mixed with wax, a plant oil such as moringa or balanites oil, and cyperus (rush-nut), ground into a viscous balm and applied to the face daily. The goal is smoother, softer-looking skin.

The recipe is described in modern reviews of the history of cosmetics, and frankincense (Boswellia) resin is also studied today for skin effects. A small 2010 split-face trial of a cream with boswellic acids reported improved fine lines and roughness after 30 days, but no trial has tested the ancient recipe itself.

paras: People who try versions of it make or buy balms combining frankincense resin or oil with beeswax and a carrier oil, applied to the face as a daily moisturiser. Modern commercial creams use Boswellia extracts instead. Anything beyond a skin-feel change is usually described over weeks.

Frankincense and its essential oil can cause contact irritation or allergy in some people, and essential oils are generally diluted in carrier oils. Steam-distilled frankincense oil does not contain boswellic acids, so it differs from extracts used in studies. People with sensitive skin are generally advised to patch-test.

angle.text: The balm is applied daily to the face with the aim of smoothing wrinkles and softening skin. A modern trial of boswellic acid cream reported improved fine lines after 30 days, though the ancient recipe itself has not been tested.

lead: The frankincense wrinkle remedy is a skincare recipe credited to ancient Egypt in which frankincense resin from Boswellia trees is combined with wax, plant oil and aromatic plant material and applied to the face to reduce the look of wrinkles [1]. It appears in cosmetic-history literature as an example of early anti-ageing practice, and in modern natural-skincare circles as a template for DIY balms.

The chain to appearance is topical: wax and oil add occlusive softness that smooths the skin surface, while frankincense is traditionally valued as a resin with soothing and aromatic properties. Modern research looks at boswellic acids, the active triterpenes in Boswellia resin, for photoaged skin [2].

A review in the Journal of Cosmetic Science describes two Egyptian recipes: one wax-based with gum, moringa oil, ground cyperus and fermented juice applied daily, and another combining frankincense gum, balanites oil, wax and rush-nut ground into a viscous fluid [1]. The specific papyrus source is not named in that review, and popular accounts that tie the recipe to Cleopatra are not documented in the sources consulted.

paras: Accounts of the remedy describe a wax base blended with frankincense gum and a plant oil, thickened with ground cyperus grass or rush-nut, producing a viscous fluid or balm rubbed onto the face daily [1]. Versions use moringa oil (Moringa oleifera) or balanites oil, and one version adds fermented plant juice [1].

Frankincense is the resin of Boswellia trees, traded across the Somali and Arabian regions for centuries; ancient Egyptians sometimes did not distinguish it from myrrh, and the Ebers Papyrus, around 1500 BCE, is among the earliest evidence of its deliberate use as a therapy [3].

Wax and oils act as emollients and occlusives, leaving skin feeling smoother, and resin adds fragrance and a protective film. Natural-skincare writers present the recipe as a heritage alternative to modern retinoids and moisturisers. Contemporary products use Boswellia extracts in serums and creams marketed for firmness and lines.

Wikipedia notes that limited clinical studies of frankincense have produced weak evidence and results are inconclusive, and that steam-distilled frankincense oils lack boswellic acids [3]. A review in Frontiers in Pharmacology describes the long traditional use of Boswellia resins for inflammatory and skin disorders [4]. A rat study reported that frankincense oil loaded into lipid nanoparticles protected against UVB photodamage [5].

No trial has tested the ancient frankincense, wax and moringa recipe. A related study used a cream containing 0.5% boswellic acids against the same cream without them in a randomised, double-blind split-face design with 15 women over 30 days; it reported significant improvement in tactile roughness and fine lines on the treated side, improved elasticity and reduced sebum, with no adverse effects [6]. The small sample and short duration limit what can be concluded.

timeline.event: The Ebers Papyrus records frankincense among medicinal plants [3].
Split-face trial of topical boswellic acids on photoaged skin published [6].
